Shareholders of The New York Times have sued the company seeking internal records concerning its oversight of Israel coverage and journalistic standards.

A Jewish former NYT employee who worked on its video desk for nearly a decade raised concerns about antisemitism, anti-Israel bias and newsroom culture at least 15 times between 2019 and her departure in March 2026, taking complaints to managers, the standards operation and HR.

She says her concerns were repeatedly dismissed and that an HR representative told her to “go find a place whose values align with yours.”

The shareholders want a judge to force the Times to produce records concerning its oversight of fact-checking, sourcing, corrections and other editorial safeguards.

The dispute began with a May 11 Nicholas Kristof column about alleged sexual abuse of Palestinian detainees in Israeli custody, before expanding to other reporting and internal complaints.

Wrong document name: A marriage license is the pre-wedding authorization. What you need afterward is a certified copy of the marriage certificate (the recorded proof the marriage happened). https://t.co/UD2FB8ClyX 

•  Not always “the town or city clerk”: Records are typically held at the county clerk/recorder or the state vital records office. You must contact the correct issuing jurisdiction. Not every county offers a simple self-service online portal on its own website. https://t.co/LksxnsFcPk 

•  Timeframe is often longer than 1–2 weeks: Standard mail requests commonly take 4–6 weeks (Iowa state office lists 4–6 weeks). text:
Two years ago, before he had played a single down at receiver in college, Reece Vander Zee was asked how the move was going to go.

"I haven't really done much receiver stuff, but hopefully it will be just like riding a bike."

Today he caught both of Iowa's touchdowns at Michigan. The second one won the game with two seconds left.

Vander Zee is from Rock Rapids, Iowa. Fewer than 3,000 people. Far northwest corner of the state.

He went to Central Lyon/George-Little Rock, a co-op high school, and he played quarterback.

As a senior he threw for 1,288 yards and 14 touchdowns and ran for 1,767 yards and 24 more.

As a junior he had played receiver instead, and caught 32 passes for 768 yards on a team that went undefeated and won state. He also made 22 tackles that year.

He won a state championship in football and another in basketball in the same school year. He lettered in four sports. Dean's List. High honor roll all four years.

The Iowa State Cyclones offered. The Nebraska Cornhuskers offered. He was never a national recruit.

He picked the Iowa Hawkeyes.

"I was on my way home, and I was like, yeah, this feels right."

And he said this about where he wanted to play.

"It doesn't matter if it's special teams or I'm playing on offense, I don't really care. I just want to get on the field."

Now here is what today actually looked like.

Iowa could not run the ball. 24 carries. 58 yards. 2.4 a carry. One rushing first down in the entire game.

The Michigan Wolverines outgained them 429 yards to 285 and held the ball for nine minutes longer.

Iowa's first touchdown was not even an offensive play. It was a 99 yard kickoff return.

So Iowa scored exactly twice on offense all afternoon, and Reece Vander Zee caught both of them. Both from 16 yards out. Both from Hank Brown, an Auburn transfer who had just been named the starter that week.

The first one tied the game at 13 in the fourth quarter.

Then Michigan went up 19-14 and missed the two point conversion. Remember that.

With two seconds on the clock at the Big House, Brown threw it 16 yards to Vander Zee again.

Iowa 20. Michigan 19.

That missed conversion is the whole margin. Michigan does the math right and the kid from Rock Rapids is just a guy who had a nice day.

Instead, No. 17 Iowa walked out of No. 18 Michigan's stadium with a one point win, and the two throws that did it both went to a former high school quarterback from a town of 3,000 who was hoping it would come back to him like riding a bike.

It did.

text:
THE RIGHT’S TOP 10  🦅

Daily News Report — September 26, 2026

Edition compiled 8:07 p.m. ET

"To be persuasive we must be believable; to be believable we must be credible; to be credible we must be truthful." — Edward R. Murrow

Purpose. This briefing organizes the day’s most consequential national headlines as they were reported and framed by leading conservative and center-right outlets. It is a synthesis, not original reporting. Claims are presented as they appeared in that coverage and, where useful, noted against same-day wire accounts so the reader can separate confirmed developments from political argument.

Source pool: major conservative-leaning and center-right outlets, including Fox News/Fox Business, Wall Street Journal, New York Post, Newsmax, Daily Wire, Breitbart, Washington Examiner, Washington Times, Just the News, National Review, and similar publications. I prioritized stories that appeared across multiple qualifying outlets or were especially prominent within the source pool. Opinion pieces and partisan commentary were generally excluded from the factual summaries.

🌍 Foreign Policy And Armed Conflict

Trump rejects Iranian ceasefire proposal as Strait of Hormuz remains central

President Donald Trump rejected an Iranian proposal for a seven-day ceasefire tied to reopening the Strait of Hormuz, saying the terms were unacceptable. Newsmax, the Washington Times, Just the News and Breitbart all prominently reported the decision, while Newsmax also reported continuing regional tensions involving Iran-backed forces.

Newsmax — Iran insists on diplomatic solution after Trump rejects peace plan

 Washington Times — Trump rejects Iranian ceasefire offer

 Just the News — Trump rejects Iran's offer to reopen Strait of Hormuz

Russia-Ukraine war continues with heavy aerial attacks
Fox News reported that Trump said approximately 25,000 people died in the Russia-Ukraine war during the previous month, following his claim of even higher casualties in the preceding month. Newsmax separately reported fresh Russian and Ukrainian strikes on September 26, including deaths in Ukraine and a Ukrainian drone attack in Russia's Krasnodar region. Trump's casualty figures are his own stated estimates and should not be treated as independently verified casualty totals.

Fox News — Trump claims stunning casualty numbers in Russia-Ukraine war

Newsmax — 7 Dead as Russia, Ukraine Exchange Strikes

U.S.-China talks produce limited trade agreement and new AI communications channel

The Trump-Xi summit produced an agreement to reduce tariffs on roughly $30 billion of goods, establish an AI-related communications channel, continue military crisis communications, and maintain negotiations over trade and rare-earth supplies. Newsmax, the Washington Times, Washington Examiner, Just the News and the New York Post all highlighted the agreements. The reports also indicate that fundamental U.S.-China disagreements remain unresolved.

Newsmax — China, US Set Up AI Safety Channel, Keep Talking Trade

Washington Examiner — U.S. and China make deal cutting tariffs on $30 billion of goods

New York Post — U.S. and China agree on $30B tariff cut

🤡 Government Dysfunction • Poor Leadership • Political Division • Corruption

White House excludes CNN from Trump's Air Force One trip

The White House excluded CNN from the press pool accompanying Trump to Tennessee on September 26. Just the News and Breitbart reported the decision, while Newsmax reported commentary defending the administration's position. The dispute comes amid a broader confrontation between the administration and several news organizations over White House access.

Just the News — White House bars CNN from Air Force One

 Breitbart — White House removes CNN from Air Force One

Trump administration attempts another nearly $1 billion funding rescission

The administration announced another roughly $1 billion in federal funding reductions, targeting programs involving immigration services, foreign assistance, education, health research and minority-owned businesses. Just the News reported that the move could face legal challenges and quoted Sen. Susan Collins arguing that the administration was infringing on Congress's appropriations authority. The White House described the spending as unnecessary or harmful.

Just the News — Trump informs Congress he will claw back another $1 billion

 Washington Examiner — Trump takes aim at DEI and noncitizen programs

Midterm politics increasingly intersects with policy controversies

The Washington Examiner reported that Republicans are confronting political challenges connected to immigration enforcement, fuel prices and other Trump-administration policies as the 2026 midterms approach. Its September 26 coverage specifically focused on Kansas ICE raids and Republican concerns about the state's Senate race. This is political reporting about the campaign environment rather than an assessment of likely election outcomes.

🛂 Immigration And The Border

ICE raids become a political issue in Kansas

The Washington Examiner reported that new ICE raids in Kansas are becoming an issue in the state's competitive Senate campaign. The reporting described Republican concerns about voter reaction to immigration enforcement while noting the historically strong Republican performance in Kansas.

Washington Examiner — Kansas ICE raids add to GOP headaches

Miami arrests highlight immigration, drugs and firearms overlap

Fox News reported that two Cuban nationals, ages 89 and 73, were arrested in Miami on allegations involving cocaine trafficking and firearms. According to court records cited by Fox, police recovered cocaine, marijuana, ammunition and stolen firearms; ICE subsequently placed detainers on the men because authorities say they had remained in the United States unlawfully for decades. The allegations remain matters for the criminal justice system.

Fox News — Illegal immigrants, 89 and 73, accused of armed drug trafficking

Human-smuggling case reported off Southern California
The New York Post reported that suspected human traffickers used vehicles to pick up migrants who arrived by boat in Newport Beach. The report described the incident as an organized smuggling operation, based partly on witness accounts.

New York Post — Human traffickers used getaway cars in Newport landing

💀 Crime • Violence • Gun Violence • Drug Addiction

Fentanyl and firearms remain a prominent law-enforcement theme

Conservative outlets continued to feature fentanyl trafficking and drug-related crime prominently. Fox News' Miami report described alleged cocaine and firearms trafficking, while other recent reporting in the source pool has focused on federal and local efforts to seize fentanyl and firearms. The September 26 coverage did not reveal a single nationally dominant crime story comparable to the Iran, China or Northeast-storm stories.

New York subway worker discovers body in utility closet

The New York Post reported that an MTA track worker discovered the body of a man believed to be in his 20s or 30s inside a utility closet in a subway tunnel near East Harlem. Authorities were investigating the circumstances surrounding the death.

New York Post — MTA worker finds dead body inside NYC subway utility closet

Crime coverage also reflects broader debate over violent-crime trends

The Washington Examiner highlighted comments from Bill Maher crediting Trump's approach as one factor in a reported decline in violent crime. Because that is an individual's interpretation rather than a standalone crime statistic, it is best treated as commentary rather than an independently established causal explanation.

🗳️ National Unity • Polarization • State Of Democracy

White House-media confrontation intensifies

The dispute over CNN's access to Air Force One was one of the clearest September 26 stories touching the relationship between government and the press. Trump also renewed criticism of CNN, Politico and MS NOW, according to Just the News, while a judge had temporarily ordered restoration of certain media credentials.

The underlying factual dispute is straightforward: which news organizations receive presidential access, under what rules, and whether those rules are being applied consistently and lawfully. The broader constitutional implications remain contested.

Midterm political polarization remains a major theme

The Washington Examiner's September 26 election coverage featured disagreements within the Republican Party over strategy, immigration enforcement and the political consequences of Trump's policies.

💸 Health Costs, Energy, And The Cost Of Living

Energy prices remain an economic concern
The Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz disruption continue to feature prominently in economic coverage because of their implications for energy markets. Washington Examiner reporting has also highlighted tensions created by high diesel prices, particularly for Republican politicians traditionally aligned with the oil industry.

Trump says new vehicle standards will lower car prices

Just the News reported Trump's announcement that he had approved new fuel-economy standards that he said would allow automakers to build vehicles at lower cost and ultimately reduce prices. The reported benefits are an administration claim rather than an independently established future outcome.

Just the News — Trump says new fuel economy standards will lead to lower vehicle prices

Consumer sentiment reflects inflation and fuel-price concerns

Breitbart reported that the University of Michigan's September consumer-sentiment reading fell to 48.1, citing rising fuel prices and inflation concerns as contributors to the deterioration in the outlook.

Breitbart — Consumer Sentiment Falls Amid Rising Inflation Worries

📉 Economy • Federal Budget Deficit • National Debt

U.S. national debt surpasses $40 trillion

Fox Business reported that the national debt stood at approximately $40.069 trillion on September 25, citing Treasury data. The figure fluctuates daily as federal receipts and expenditures are recorded.

Fox Business — U.S. national debt tracker

Tariffs and trade remain central to the economic outlook

The new U.S.-China agreement reduces tariffs on a limited group of goods while maintaining broader negotiations over trade and rare-earth supplies. The Washington Examiner and Newsmax both emphasized that the agreement is narrower than a comprehensive resolution of the U.S.-China trade dispute.

Grocery companies reduce product lineups amid changing consumer conditions

The Washington Times reported that Coca-Cola and PepsiCo are trimming portions of their snack and beverage lineups in 2026 as companies respond to changing consumer demand and market conditions.

Washington Times — Coca-Cola, PepsiCo trim snack and juice lineups

🏚️ Poverty • Homelessness • Related Social Issues

No single poverty or homelessness story clearly matched the prominence of the Iran conflict, U.S.-China agreement, Northeast storm, national-debt story, or White House-media dispute in the September 26 conservative/center-right source pool I reviewed.

The broader social-policy coverage was instead concentrated on immigration-related government spending, education controversies and the cost pressures associated with inflation and energy. The administration's attempted rescission of nearly $1 billion included programs serving refugees and unaccompanied minors, making it relevant to this category as well as government spending.

🌩️ Additional Major Story: Northeast Nor'easter

Although it does not fit neatly into the requested categories, the powerful nor'easter hitting the East Coast was one of the day's most prominent domestic stories in the conservative news ecosystem.

The New York Post reported that the storm killed a Brooklyn man and left more than 100,000 homes without power across the region. Fox Weather reported severe coastal flooding, heavy rain, beach erosion and wind gusts reaching roughly 50–60 mph in parts of New England, with tens of millions of people affected or potentially affected.

New York Post — Violent nor'easter hammers NYC and surrounding region

 Fox Weather — Powerful nor'easter lashes the East Coast

📝 Overall Daily Summary

September 26's conservative and center-right news coverage was dominated by foreign policy, the Iran conflict, the Strait of Hormuz and the aftermath of the Trump-Xi summit. Trump's rejection of Iran's proposed ceasefire kept the Middle East conflict at the center of geopolitical coverage, while Russia and Ukraine continued exchanging strikes. The U.S.-China summit produced tangible but limited agreements on tariffs, AI communications and military crisis management, giving the day's economic and foreign-policy coverage a second major focus. At home, the confrontation between the White House and news organizations over press access remained a significant story about the relationship between government and the media. Immigration enforcement continued to generate political and law-enforcement coverage, including ICE activity in Kansas and criminal cases involving undocumented immigrants. Economic reporting emphasized the $40 trillion national debt, inflation concerns, fuel prices and trade policy, while a major nor'easter produced significant flooding, wind damage and power outages along the East Coast. Overall, the day's qualifying coverage was characterized by a combination of international conflict, contentious executive-branch actions, immigration enforcement, political polarization, energy pressures and persistent fiscal concerns.

text:
Before the expansion of the Roman Republic/Empire and Christianization (which spread Roman law and southern/Mediterranean monotheism), northern and central Europe (Celtic, Germanic, Nordic and Baltic peoples) had a completely customary, oral, decentralized and restorative justice system.
1. Based on oral habit and memory
Instead of written laws enacted by a king or senate, the law was conceived as pre-existing and sacred, transmitted through verbal tradition.
Specialized jurists: In the Celtic world there were Brehones (brithem), judges who memorized jurisprudence in poetic verse to facilitate its transmission. In the Nordic and Germanic countries there was the figure of the Lögsögumaður ("law decider"), who memorized the memory code and recited it before the assembly.
2. The Community Assembly (Thing or Mallus)
Justice did not reside in a court or monarch, but in the popular assembly of free men.
The Thing (or Ting): It was the central institution of the Germanic and Scandinavian peoples. These mass outdoor gatherings judged crimes, resolved territorial disputes and concluded alliances.
There was no public "police force"; enforcement of sentences depended on the aggrieved person's own social support or family.
3. Restorative rather than punitive justice
Unlike Roman tradition or the modern state model (which seeks to imprison or punish the inmate on behalf of the state), the main objective of the north was to restore social balance between clans.
The Wergild (man's blood payment/price): If someone committed murder or inflicted an injury, they did not go to jail; they had to pay financial or livestock compensation to the victim's family.
The "Honor Price" or Lóg n-enech (in Celtic Brehon Laws): Each member of society had a value assigned according to his social status and role. An offense or crime against a high-status person required greater compensation.
Avoiding blood vendetta (feud): Paying these fines prevented clans from destroying each other in endless wars.
4. The Outlaw (Outlawry)
For crimes deemed treacherous or aberrant (such as treasonous murder or serious cowardice), or when a defendant refused to accept the Thing's sentence, the supreme punishment was banishment or banishment.
By outlawing someone (skóggangr or declaring outlaw), they were stripped of all legal status. He was left out of the tribe's protection, so anyone could kill him with impunity and no one could offer him shelter or food.
5. Evidence: Oaths and Judgments of God (Ordeals)
In the absence of forensic evidence, the evidentiary process was based on:
Purchase: The defendant was to assemble a group of "co-jurers" (oath-helpers) who solemnly swore by the local gods or their ancestors about the defendant's honesty.
Ordeals: If oral evidence was not enough, divine judgment was appealed to (walking on embers, dipping your arm in boiling water), believing that the forces of nature or the gods would intervene to save the innocent.
To delve deeper into the evolution of these ancient systems, this historical analysis addresses the workings of traditional Celtic laws before external influence:
The Spirit of the Law? What Irish Mythology Can Teach
This video examines in detail how Brehon Laws operated in pre-provincial Ireland, focusing on their community structure, the absence of prisons and the principle of honour restitution.

text:
Brian needs to sit this one out. He managed Ireland V Russia as Russia were busy bludgeoning their way through what remained of the Chechnya resistance while merrily throwing every man woman and child who happened to be in the way into the woodchipper. 

And Brian? There wasn’t a fucking peep out of him then, not the merest throat clearing or condemnation of Russia. 

Furthermore, as Ireland international manager Brian took Ireland to play in Tel Aviv against Israel, and he also managed Ireland against Israel in Dublin, failing to win either tie at a time when Ireland was blessed with considerably greater playing talent than Israel had at their disposal. This, at a time when Israel actually occupied Gaza and had settlements there, which they had maintained since their victory in the six-day war in the 1960s. If that bothered Brian, he kept it to himself very well.

This social conscience he's sprouted since stepping down as the table bottoming manager of the Faroe Islands was conspicuous by its absence when he still made his living from football. Yet here he is in 2026 doing his best Mahatma Ghandi impression while shouting the odds in the face of those whose only crime is to harbour a desire to have a shot at what he had when he still had something to offer the game.

The biggest blessing Brian enjoyed in his professional career, one he should be thankful for but isn't, was that he never had to contend with bitter resentful has-beens demanding that he take a hit to his career to satisfy their narcissistic messiah complexes. 

I know from reading the above it might appear that I have a very low opinion of Brian Kerr. but I don't. Ultimately, I think Brian probably does have reasonable grounds to be bitter towards the FAI. His contribution to Irish football is substantial, and I'm sure I'm not the only one who thought that the FAI dispensed with his services. with unreasonable haste. Brian was also a brilliant manager at club level. In his own way, he was also inspirational. to young players and coaches in Ireland.

I wish we still had that version of Brian Kerr. 

￼

text:
Both parties broke our immigration system. Both parties must finally fix it.

For decades, Washington has offered Americans the same dishonest choice: accept chaos at the border or accept mass deportations that tear apart families and communities. I reject both.

I was nineteen when my first Navy mission involved helping rescue Cuban families fleeing Castro’s dictatorship during the Mariel Boatlift. I learned early that border security and human dignity are not competing principles. A strong country can enforce its laws without abandoning its values.

My plan would modernize surveillance at the southern border and in the Florida Straits, strengthen our ports of entry, and improve coordination among federal and local law enforcement. It would focus enforcement resources on violent criminals, traffickers, cartels, smugglers, repeat offenders, and national-security threats—not peaceful families who are working, paying taxes, and raising American children.

It would also add immigration judges, asylum officers, investigators, and interpreters so cases can be decided quickly and fairly. People with legitimate claims should not wait years for an answer. Neither should the government.

For longtime residents, I support an earned, renewable legal status—not automatic citizenship or federal benefits. Applicants would undergo background checks, pay applicable taxes, fees, and penalties, meet English and civics requirements, and remain in good standing under the law.

People who entered through legal humanitarian programs must receive notice, due process, and an orderly review before the government changes their status. Immigration enforcement must also be professional and accountable, with clear identification, appropriate body-camera requirements, independent inspections, medical care in detention, access to counsel, and consequences for misconduct.

Finally, employers who traffic workers, steal wages, or knowingly exploit unauthorized labor must be held responsible. Law enforcement cannot punish workers while giving the businesses profiting from a broken system a free pass.

South Florida understands immigration in a way Washington never has. We believe in law and order because many of our families escaped places where the law protected the regime instead of the people. We believe in legal immigration because we know what the chance to become an American can mean.

Secure the border. Enforce the law. Protect the innocent. Keep America’s word.

That is the bipartisan immigration plan I will take to Congress.

text:
Alan Kay argued that people who are really serious about software should make their own hardware, and now is the time. But AI demands much tighter integration between hardware and software. Without device-level access, the full potential of AI agents cannot be unlocked. 

Think of Doubao. AI demands a level of hardware-software intimacy that traditional software never really needed. Hardware is no longer just the box AI happens to run on; it is how an agent acquires context, permissions, senses, and ultimately the ability to act. Your phone knows your social life, your PC and tablet know your work, and your glasses can see the world you are actually standing in. So when tech companies race to own phones, PCs, tablets, and glasses, they are competing to assemble the most complete version of you.

Doubao, however, reveals the awkward catch: owning the OS does not mean owning what happens inside the apps. An agent may have deep access to Android, but if WeChat, Alipay, and Meituan refuse to play along, a surprisingly large part of digital life remains behind locked doors. GUI agents tried the brute-force approach—if there is no API, just click the buttons like a human—but unsurprisingly, security and risk-control systems were not thrilled. MCP and A2A offer a much cleaner path by standardizing how agents interact with services, but protocols cannot force an app to open its gates. The mobile internet spent the last fifteen years building walled gardens; AI agents are now discovering just how high those walls really are.

"From veteran Financial Times journalist Robin Wigglesworth, an epic history of the debt that built the modern world.

Long considered the "boring" corner of finance, bonds are anything but. They have funded everything from the Crusades to climate tech, Netflix series to AI data centers. They are now bigger than the stock market and rival even the global banking system in influence. They are also misunderstood—treated as mere debt, when in fact their form, function, and impact are radically different.

In A Fabulous Debt, Robin Wigglesworth. The Financial Times’ Global Finance Correspondent, and author of the acclaimed Trillions offers a sweeping, affectionate history of the bond market. From the dyke-builders of 17th-century Holland to the trillion-dollar portfolios of BlackRock, this is a people’s history of finance: rich in drama, full of colorful characters, and bursting with insight.

With clarity and wit, Wigglesworth takes readers from medieval Venice to modern Wall Street, tracing how bonds evolved from obscure financial instruments into the invisible architecture of the modern world. Along the way, we meet warlords and water boards, merchant princes and mathematicians, financiers and fraudsters all of whom helped build the most powerful machine in global finance.

This isn’t just a book about the past. It's a guide to the present and future of the financial system and a love letter to the engine that keeps it running."

📺 " Larry King: The UFO Cover-Up? Live from Area 51 (1994) Full Version, Good Quality, Commercial-Free "
🔗 https://t.co/iajp1NeTCk

📝 “The UFO Cover-Up? Live from Area 51” — Larry King, TNT, October 1, 1994

Watching this television special in its entirety today is like opening a genuine time capsule of early-1990s UFO research and culture.

This is much more than an old television program about UFOs. In roughly an hour and a half, it brings together — either live, through prerecorded interviews, or through archival footage — an extraordinary collection of people representing almost every major side of the UFO debate at the time: UFO researchers, skeptics, scientists, military witnesses, politicians, activists, journalists, and figures from popular culture.

The special was broadcast on October 1, 1994, with Larry King reporting from Rachel, Nevada, near Area 51.

Its structure is particularly valuable historically. A central panel participates live, while a series of prerecorded reports dramatically expands the range of people and subjects covered throughout the program.

The Live Panel

Larry King is joined by four very different figures.

Dr. Steven M. Greer, an emergency physician and founder of CSETI, openly discusses the extraterrestrial hypothesis, his own claimed close-range observations, and his group's attempts to establish communication through light signals. He argues that at least one extraterrestrial civilization has reached Earth and advocates attempting some form of peaceful communication or diplomatic relationship.

Stanton T. Friedman, nuclear physicist and veteran UFO researcher, argues strongly that some UFOs are extraterrestrial spacecraft and describes what he calls a “Cosmic Watergate”: a system of secrecy in which only a relatively small number of people within government would possess the complete information.

Friedman discusses several possible reasons for such secrecy: military and technological advantage, national security, competition with other nations, economic consequences, and the possible social impact of an official announcement confirming extraterrestrial visitation.

Captain Kevin Randle, a U.S. Air Force Reserve officer and Roswell researcher, concentrates heavily on the 1947 Roswell incident, its witnesses, the recovered material, and the explanations subsequently offered by the Air Force.

Glenn Campbell, an Area 51 researcher and activist, brings the discussion into the present of 1994: Groom Lake, classified installations, desert surveillance, sensors, security patrols, secret aircraft programs, and the difficulty of separating possible advanced terrestrial technology from UFO interpretations.

These four men alone represent several substantially different approaches to the same mystery.

But the Real Historical Richness Lies Beyond the Live Panel

Carefully watching the prerecorded segments reveals an extraordinary number of people who became important figures in the history of UFO research, skepticism, science, politics, and popular culture.

At 2:06, we identified Richard Schickel, appearing during the opening discussion about UFOs, movies, mythology, and the human imagination.

At 3:02, Carl Sagan appears, representing one of the most important scientific and skeptical perspectives in the program.

At 3:50, we see Jacques Vallée, whose interpretation of the phenomenon is considerably more complex than a simple “extraterrestrials versus no extraterrestrials” debate.

At 5:39, William Shatner, forever associated with Captain James T. Kirk and Star Trek, discusses the powerful influence of science fiction and the human desire to believe in other intelligences.

At 6:39, we identified prominent UFO skeptic Philip J. Klass.

At 18:13, the program introduces “Agent X” — Mark Farmer, a researcher associated with monitoring secret aerospace projects.

At 21:03, we see Rep. James H. Bilbray of Nevada.

Later, during the Roswell material, we identified Robert Shirkey at 35:01, Walter Haut at 35:28, and George “Jud” Roberts at 35:50.

And then, at 37:01, appears Rep. Steven H. Schiff of New Mexico.

His presence is historically significant because Schiff was, at that very moment, pursuing answers about government records concerning Roswell. The GAO investigation he requested had begun in February 1994 and was still underway when this program aired. Its final report would not be issued until July 28, 1995.

So we are not watching Schiff retrospectively describing a completed historical investigation.

We are watching him while the investigation is actually taking place.

Throughout the rest of the program we also encounter Barry Goldwater, Robert O. Dean, Budd Hopkins, Don Ecker, Linda Moulton Howe, Jenny Randles, Ed Komarek, Mindy Garber, and others, along with archival footage of Ronald Reagan.

That is an extraordinary concentration of people in a single television production.

Roswell at a Crucial Historical Moment

Roswell inevitably occupies a central position.

The program revisits the July 1947 announcement from Roswell Army Air Field that personnel had recovered a “flying disc,” followed shortly afterward by the explanation that the recovered object was a balloon.

The prerecorded material includes several people directly or indirectly connected with the historical case.

Walter Haut was the Public Information Officer at the 509th Bomb Group who distributed the original 1947 “flying disc” press release.

Robert Shirkey had been assigned to base operations with the 509th Bomb Group in 1947 and later made claims about seeing material being transported aboard a B-29.

George “Jud” Roberts, manager and minority shareholder of Roswell radio station KGFL, stated that his station recorded an interview with rancher W.W. “Mac” Brazel and that he subsequently received a warning concerning its release.

The program therefore preserves testimony from people whose names are deeply connected with the development of the Roswell story.

And the timing of the broadcast is crucial.

Only months earlier, the Air Force had completed a new investigation and concluded that the most likely source of the recovered material was a balloon train associated with the then-classified Project MOGUL, which was designed to help detect Soviet nuclear activity.

Randle and Friedman challenge aspects of that explanation during the program.

This makes the special particularly valuable historically: we are seeing the Roswell controversy during a period when major official and congressional investigations were actively unfolding, rather than through the lens of everything that happened afterward.

Area 51, Groom Lake and Secret Technology

Another enormous subject is Area 51 itself.

The program discusses Groom Lake, restricted access, warning signs, unmarked security vehicles, electronic sensors in the desert, classified aircraft development, stealth technology and rumored aerospace programs such as Aurora.

This leads to one of the most important questions running through the entire special:

How many extraordinary sightings might actually represent classified human technology — and what, if anything, remains unexplained after those cases are removed?

Even among the panelists interested in UFOs, there is no single answer.

Toward the end, Kevin Randle says he believes Area 51 is probably being used for development of the next generation of military aircraft and that he does not personally think extraterrestrial evidence is necessarily stored there.

Greer, meanwhile, says that he does not actually know what is happening at Area 51.

That distinction is important.

Wright-Patterson, Barry Goldwater and General Curtis LeMay

One of the most historically valuable prerecorded appearances is that of former U.S. Senator and 1964 presidential candidate Barry Goldwater.

Goldwater says he believes the government knows more about UFOs, while explicitly acknowledging that he cannot prove it.

He then recounts his famous encounter with General Curtis LeMay.

Goldwater says he asked LeMay whether he could enter a room at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base where, according to what Goldwater had heard, secret UFO-related material was kept.

According to Goldwater, LeMay became extremely angry and told him never to ask that question again.

This recording is particularly valuable because it allows us to distinguish what Goldwater himself actually said from stronger versions of the story that circulated later.

In this program, Goldwater does not say that LeMay told him extraterrestrial bodies were stored there.

He does not say LeMay told him alien wreckage was stored there.

He does not recount a threat of court-martial.

And, crucially, he does not say that LeMay told him that LeMay himself was unable to enter the room.

But then something extremely interesting happens.

Later, Larry King asks the live panel what LeMay's angry response to Goldwater might have meant.

Steven Greer replies that he has spoken with Barry Goldwater and says that, “from what I understand,” Curtis LeMay himself did not have access to the area where this material was allegedly kept.

That distinction matters enormously.

Within the same 1994 program we therefore have:

Goldwater's direct account → Larry King's question → Greer's additional interpretation/information.

For anyone studying the genealogy of the Goldwater-LeMay story, this may be one of the most interesting sections of the entire broadcast.

Robert O. Dean and Military Testimony

Robert O. Dean, a retired military figure who became well known in UFO circles, appears repeatedly.

His presence brings another major theme of early-1990s ufology into the program: former military personnel claiming to have encountered classified information concerning UFOs.

Importantly, the production does not simply present these claims in isolation.

Statements from witnesses and UFO researchers are repeatedly juxtaposed with skeptical commentary from Sagan, Klass and others.

That tension is one reason the program remains historically useful.

Budd Hopkins and the Alien-Abduction Era

No portrait of American ufology in the late 1980s and early 1990s would be complete without alien abductions.

Budd Hopkins represents this major branch of UFO research.

The program examines accounts from people who claimed that they had been abducted, subjected to procedures or examinations and subsequently returned.

It also raises questions concerning memory, interpretation and the enormous difficulty of establishing objective evidence for extraordinary personal experiences.

The prominence given to the subject demonstrates just how central the abduction phenomenon had become within American UFO culture by 1994.

Linda Moulton Howe and Cattle Mutilations

With Linda Moulton Howe, another major branch of the UFO mystery enters the program: anomalous animal deaths, documentation, witness testimony and the alleged relationship between UFO activity and cattle mutilations.

The subject even returns during the live viewer calls.

A caller from Colorado asks about cattle mutilations, producing sharply different explanations from the panelists, ranging from possible military or intelligence involvement to predominantly natural causes.

Again, there is no unified “UFO believer” position.

Carl Sagan and Philip Klass: Skepticism Is Part of the Historical Record

The appearances of Carl Sagan and Philip Klass make the film even more valuable.

Sagan emphasizes the necessity of distinguishing fact from fiction and hope from reality.

The fundamental issue is not whether extraterrestrial life could exist, but whether the evidence being presented actually establishes the extraordinary conclusions being drawn from it.

Klass represents an even more strongly skeptical position toward many UFO claims.

Their presence is essential because this broadcast preserves not only the arguments of UFO proponents but also those of two of the most prominent critics associated with the subject at the time.

Jacques Vallée and a Third Possibility

Jacques Vallée is particularly fascinating because his position does not fit comfortably into either camp.

Early in the program he discusses the possibility of a form of non-human consciousness associated with the phenomenon and its apparent presence throughout human history.

Later he proposes another striking possibility: perhaps the cover-up is principally a “cover-up of ignorance rather than knowledge.”

In other words, governments might sometimes conceal information not because they possess all the answers, but because they do not understand the phenomenon themselves and have little incentive to admit publicly that something may exist beyond their control or comprehension.

That is a very different interpretation of secrecy.

Government Documents and the Problem of Secrecy

One of the strongest later segments asks a simple question.

If the Air Force officially ended Project Blue Book in 1969, why do later government documents continue to contain references to UFO-related incidents or concepts?

The program discusses a classified 1979 document concerning a reported UFO incident in Bolivia, a CIA paper containing a reference to a possible UFO propulsion system, and the NSA's efforts to resist the release of certain UFO records.

The program does not establish that these documents prove extraterrestrial visitation.

Instead, it raises a narrower but important historical question:

How extensive was government interest in UFO reports after the official termination of Project Blue Book, and why were some records still classified or withheld?

Ronald Reagan and the Extraterrestrial-Threat Analogy

Archival footage of President Ronald Reagan is also used.

Reagan famously speculated about how quickly humanity's differences might disappear if the world faced an external threat from beyond Earth.

The program presents the provocative question: was Reagan merely using a rhetorical thought experiment, or did his remarks mean something more?

But importantly, the narration later warns against automatically treating such statements as evidence of hidden UFO knowledge.

It is a good example of the central problem running throughout the entire special:

evidence versus interpretation.

UFO Activism Before Today's Disclosure Movement

The film even documents public activism demanding greater government transparency concerning UFOs.

We identified Ed Komarek and Mindy Garber during the protest/sit-in sequence.

Seen from the perspective of 2026, this material is particularly interesting.

Public demands for the release of UFO files, greater transparency and what would increasingly be called Disclosure were already visible and organized more than three decades ago — long before social media, smartphones and today's UAP debate.

The “Curtain of Ridicule”

Another theme running through the entire program is stigma.

During the final viewer calls, Randle describes what he calls a “curtain of ridicule.”

As long as people fear being mocked for reporting what they have seen, potentially valuable witnesses may remain silent.

At the same time, the program acknowledges the opposite problem: sensationalism, unreliable stories, exaggerated claims and premature conclusions can make serious investigation extraordinarily difficult.

Those two problems reinforce each other.

It is one of the most contemporary aspects of this 1994 broadcast.

What Would Happen After Confirmation?

The program does not merely ask:

“Are UFOs real?”

It also asks a much larger question:

What would happen to human civilization if extraterrestrial visitation were officially confirmed?

Friedman speculates about religious, psychological, economic and political consequences. He suggests that younger generations might begin to think of themselves less as Americans, Chinese or Canadians and more simply as Earthlings.

Greer imagines confirmation as a potentially catalytic event capable of pushing civilization toward a more global perspective.

Campbell is much more pragmatic: even after an extraordinary revelation and an enormous media reaction, people would eventually return to their jobs and everyday lives.

Three very different answers to a question that is still being debated today.

Even the Coming Camera Revolution Is Anticipated

Near the end of the broadcast, the increasing availability of video cameras and other technologies is discussed as something that could make future UFO events increasingly difficult to dismiss.

From the perspective of 2026, this is fascinating.

In 1994, billions of people carrying high-resolution digital cameras in their pockets was still science fiction.

Yet the underlying question remains surprisingly relevant:

Does having more cameras necessarily produce better evidence?

Why This Video Matters

The historical importance of The UFO Cover-Up? Live from Area 51 does not depend on accepting the conclusions of any participant.

Its importance is documentary.

In a single surviving television program we encounter:

Larry King, Steven M. Greer, Stanton T. Friedman, Kevin Randle, Glenn Campbell, Richard Schickel, Carl Sagan, Jacques Vallée, William Shatner, Philip J. Klass, Mark Farmer (“Agent X”), Rep. James H. Bilbray, Robert Shirkey, Walter Haut, George “Jud” Roberts, Rep. Steven H. Schiff, Barry Goldwater, Robert O. Dean, Budd Hopkins, Don Ecker, Linda Moulton Howe, Jenny Randles, Ed Komarek, Mindy Garber, and Ronald Reagan through archival footage.

And around those people we find an extraordinary cross-section of early-1990s UFO subjects:

Roswell; Project MOGUL; Area 51; Groom Lake; secret aerospace programs; alleged reverse engineering; crash-retrieval claims; alleged bodies and wreckage; Wright-Patterson; Goldwater and LeMay; government documents; the NSA and CIA; military testimony; alien abductions; cattle mutilations; crop circles; attempts at extraterrestrial contact; CSETI; scientific skepticism; witness credibility; government secrecy; public access to classified records; Disclosure; the social consequences of possible contact; and the future role of video technology in documenting the phenomenon.

But perhaps the most fascinating aspect is something else.

Watching it today gives us something the original audience could never have possessed:

more than three decades of hindsight.

We see Steven Schiff discussing Roswell while the GAO investigation is still underway.

We see Barry Goldwater personally recounting his encounter with Curtis LeMay.

We see Steven Greer, in 1994, adding an important element to that story that Goldwater himself does not state in the recorded account.

We see Carl Sagan participating in the debate.

We see Jacques Vallée articulating ideas that would continue to be discussed decades later.

We see activists demanding that government UFO files be opened.

We see researchers discussing stigma, secrecy and the need for greater transparency.

And we hear predictions about how new recording technology might eventually transform the UFO evidence problem.

For that reason, describing this simply as an old television program about UFOs would greatly underestimate its value.

It is a historical document of American ufology in 1994.

It preserves what people knew, what they claimed to know, what they suspected, what skeptics challenged — and, perhaps most importantly, what remained unknown on October 1, 1994.

That is why this video deserves to be watched again slowly, person by person, statement by statement.

Because today we can do something that Larry King's audience in 1994 could not:

compare what these people were saying then with everything that emerged during the following three decades.

text:
The founder of America's most famous Black town gave away a hundred and twenty-three thousand Black votes to keep it. His name was Isaiah Montgomery, he was the only Black delegate in that Jackson hall in 1890, and Frederick Douglass called it treason four months later.

Every viral post about Mound Bayou leaves this part out, which means the whole thing has been handed to you backward. Go find out what the man actually said that day, because it is not what you think.

One man wanted his town left alone. To get it he stood up in a hall in Jackson in the summer of 1890 and offered Mississippi the ballots of a hundred and twenty-three thousand Black men.

He was the only Black delegate in the room. He was also the founder of Mound Bayou.

Three years before that, in the fall of 1887, Isaiah Montgomery had walked a small group of men off a train into a stand of hardwood in Bolivar County. Booker T. Washington wrote down what happened next and published it in 1907.

Montgomery waved a hand toward the trees. This is a pretty wild place, he told them.

The men looked where he was pointing and said nothing.

But this whole country was like this once, he went on. You have seen it change, and you and your fathers performed most of the work that made it what it is.

Then the line that ends the scene in Washington's telling. You and your fathers did this for some one else, he said, so can't you do as much now for yourselves?

The men picked up their axes and went at the wilderness.

That is where the retellings stop. The next five years cost more than anybody puts in a caption.

Fewer than seventy-five acres of the tract could be planted. The rest was cane and hardwood so thick a man went through it with a hatchet.

Swamp fever got some of them. There were bears and panthers in the timber, so men stood watch while other men cut.

Simon Gaiter arrived with a hundred and seventy-five dollars. That was every cent he had in the world, and after he paid for his land and his provisions he had ten dollars left.

For years the settlement lived off what it chopped down. They sold the timber as cross ties and staves to the same railroad that held their notes.

Some sharecropped on the side to stay afloat. Some sent their wives and children out to pick cotton for white planters and clean white people's houses, which is how they kept the wolf from the door.

At the end of five years a good many of them still owed the railroad money. Montgomery was one of them.

On the twelfth of August, 1890, one hundred and thirty-four men sat down in a Jackson hall in the deep of a Mississippi summer to write the state a new constitution.

The convention president, S. S. Calhoon, had already said out loud what the body was for. They had come to exclude the Negro, he said, and nothing short of that would answer.

A white delegate from Jasper County named Marsh Cook had run on Black voting rights. He was killed on a country road, riding alone, before he could take his seat.

Judge J. J. Chrisman sat in that hall and said out loud that there had not been a full vote and a fair count in Mississippi since 1875. He is also on record crying out whether there was to be no higher ambition for the young white men of the South than keeping the Negro down.

His name went on the finished document.

Montgomery was forty-three. He weighed maybe a hundred and thirty-five pounds, and they had seated him on the franchise committee, the one holding the pen.

He spoke for about an hour. The phrase he used was that he was laying the suffrage of his fellow men at the feet of this convention.

Give the vote only to men who can read, he argued, and call them the stable and prudent element among the citizens. He knew better than any man in that room whose fathers had been forbidden by law to learn their letters.

His reasoning was not stupid and it was not sudden. The ballot in Mississippi had already been taken by fraud and by gunfire, and he believed trading a right nobody was permitted to use might buy his people a generation of quiet.

Two weeks later he told a northern newspaper it did not wholly suit him. It was the best that could be done, he said, and they had to take the best they could get.

The New York World printed the address that September.

In October, Frederick Douglass stood up at Metropolitan African Methodist Episcopal Church in Washington and called it treason to the cause of the colored people. He also said he had heard inside it a groan of bitter anguish, and the voice of a soul from which all hope had gone.

Both of those things were true at the same time. Douglass was old enough to hold them together.

Mound Bayou got what it was bought for.

The town incorporated in 1898 with about a hundred and eighty registered voters, in a state where walking up to a registrar could get a Black man killed. It got a bank in 1904, three cotton gins, a sawmill, a train station and its own schools.

Its Carnegie library was the one institution in town that white people ran. That part never makes the posts.

Theodore Roosevelt had his train stopped there. From the platform he called it an object lesson full of hope for the colored people and therefore full of hope for the white people, too.

Booker T. Washington came in November 1912 to open the cottonseed oil mill. Delta families had bought into it at a dollar a share.

Outside the town line the arithmetic ran the other way. By the 1892 elections the new registration lists in Mississippi carried about seventy thousand white voters and about nine thousand Black ones.

Something like fifty-two thousand white men lost the vote as well. Black registration fell from better than nine in ten voting-age men during Reconstruction to fewer than six in a hundred.

Then cotton prices dropped and the shelter started leaking. State examiners closed the Bank of Mound Bayou in 1914.

To rescue the oil mill the town brought in Benjamin B. Harvey, a white cotton man out of Memphis who was to lease the plant and keep up the bond payments. He took the money, and the mill stood empty for years.

The dollar shares went with it.

Montgomery lived another thirty-four years and never took back a word of the speech in public. In a private letter to Booker T. Washington he admitted what he had worked out.

The men talking about pure government wanted Black Mississippians pushed back toward serfdom. Nothing short of federal force was going to stop them.

He died in March 1924. A white planter and politician named Walter Sillers gave the eulogy.

The tomb they laid him in was paid for by a subscription taken up among white men.

A missionary passing through wrote that no Black Mississippian was hated by Black people more than he was. The men who collected for that tomb were the only ones who ever got what they came for.

The town did not go into the ground with him.

A fire tore through the business district in the early 1940s and took most of what was left of the storefronts. The next thing built on that ground was a hospital.

In 1942 the Knights and Daughters of Tabor opened a forty-two bed hospital on the highway. Twenty-five thousand members, most of them sharecroppers, had paid for it out of their own assessments.

Perry M. Smith had gone plantation to plantation collecting it a little at a time.

By 1944, dues of eight dollars and forty cents a year bought a member thirty-one days of care, surgery included. Every doctor and every nurse in that building was Black, and a Black patient walked in the front door and was seen.

Between 1942 and 1964 that hospital treated more than a hundred and thirty-five thousand people.

In 1951 its chief surgeon, T. R. M. Howard, started the Regional Council of Negro Leadership in Mound Bayou. The next year a young insurance salesman named Medgar Evers moved to town to work for him.

The council's rallies pulled ten thousand people into a town of a couple thousand. Myrlie Evers described them as an all-day camp meeting, part pep rally, part revival, part Sunday church picnic.

Fannie Lou Hamer sat in those crowds, and so did Amzie Moore and Aaron Henry. They ran voter registration drives out of the one town in Mississippi whose founder had helped write the rules against them.

The town was carrying a higher NAACP membership, measured against its Black population, than anywhere else in Mississippi, and the bargain had been meant to keep it quiet.

In September 1955 Howard's house on the edge of town filled with people who could not safely close their eyes anywhere else in Mississippi. Emmett Till's mother slept there, and so did Congressman Charles Diggs, the Black reporters covering the trial, and the witnesses.

Armed guards worked the property around the clock and the house was full of weapons. Mississippi would not issue a Black man a permit to carry, so Howard drove with a pistol in a compartment built into his car.

More than once that year he was carried out of a meeting inside a casket, because a hearse was the one vehicle nobody stopped and searched.

At night Howard and Medgar Evers and the Black press went out on the county roads looking for people who had seen something. In the courthouse at Sumner the sheriff greeted those same reporters every morning with a slur.

After the first day of the trial they gathered in Howard's front room. Medgar Evers was there, and Ruby Hurley of the NAACP, and three newspapermen named James Hicks, L. Alex Wilson and Simeon Booker.

The reporters wanted to run what they had that night. Howard made them sit on it until the witnesses were somewhere safe.

One of those witnesses was an eighteen-year-old named Willie Reed.

He was a sharecropper's grandson out of Drew. He had watched two white men drive a boy into a barn on the Milam place, and he had heard what went on inside it.

One of those men had already come and stood in front of him and asked whether he had seen anything. No, sir, he said.

Did you hear anything, boy. No, sir.

On the morning of the twenty-second he walked out of Howard's house, rode the forty-two miles to Sumner, went through the crowd at the courthouse door and named J. W. Milam and Roy Bryant out loud in a Mississippi courtroom.

The jury took sixty-seven minutes. He was moved out of the state within days.

Ten years after that, the money came from a direction nobody in 1890 could have imagined.

In 1965 a doctor named Jack Geiger got federal War on Poverty funding to build two community health centers, one in Boston and one in the Delta. He put the Delta one in Mound Bayou, and it opened its doors to patients in 1967.

It was the first rural community health center in the United States. The federally funded community health center system this country runs on traces back to that clinic and its sister project in Boston.

The staff dug wells. They set pumps, built privies, cut drainage ditches and screened people's windows, because in the Delta the water and the flies were the disease.

Then Geiger started writing prescriptions for meat, milk, vegetables and fruit. People filled them at the grocery store, and the grocers sent the bills to the health center.

He paid them out of the pharmacy budget.

Washington sent a man down to tell him he could not buy groceries with health center money. Geiger told him that the last time he looked in his textbooks, the specific therapy for malnutrition was food.

Two Black farmers in Mound Bayou donated land, and the center turned it into a four hundred and twenty-seven acre cooperative farm.

John Hatch, who helped build it, put it plainly. These were people sitting on top of the richest soil in the nation, going hungry, who already knew how to grow food.

The woman they put in charge of those acres was named L. C. Dorsey. She had grown up on a Delta plantation picking other people's cotton, and she would end up running the whole health center from 1988 to 1995.

She said later that it was not a plantation named Tufts you were working for. This was your land.

Isaiah Montgomery had stood in a forest in 1887 and asked a handful of men whether they could do for themselves what their fathers had done for somebody else. Eighty years later he got his answer.

A hundred and twenty-three thousand ballots laid at the feet of a convention in 1890. A hundred and thirty-five thousand Delta patients through the doors of the Taborian between 1942 and 1964.

The record kept Isaiah Montgomery. It lost nearly every man who swung an axe at that forest.

What few names it did hold onto, like Simon Gaiter and his ten dollars, sit in books almost nobody opens.

So when Mound Bayou comes across your feed as a miracle in the swamp, put those men in the sentence with him. The founder made the deal, and they paid the bill for it in blisters and swamp fever and other people's cotton.

The Taborian is shuttered. Montgomery's house stands empty with the foundation cracked, and the town is down around fifteen hundred people.

On the far south side of Chicago, sometime in the early seventies, an orderly and a nurse's aide lifted a patient onto a gurney.

The orderly asked her for a kiss. She walked around to the other side of the bed and kissed him on the jaw.

His name was Willie Louis, which was not the name he was born with. He had been eighteen the last night he slept in Mound Bayou, and he had not said the other name out loud since.

text:
Hey, y’all. I did some moon gazing and a quick reading tonight, and I want to share what came through. As always, this won’t resonate with everybody. Take what speaks to you and leave what doesn’t.

I’m picking up on somebody from the past, or someone connected to them, coming forward with an invitation. If that happens, pause before you say yes. Ask yourself whether being around this person would bring peace into your life or pull you back into drama. Think about your finances, your headspace, and whether you feel emotionally and physically safe. You don’t have to accept an invitation just because it was offered.

I also got a reminder to spend some time in nature. Take a walk, sit outside, breathe, and listen to yourself. If you’ve been in hermit mode, this may be your nudge to put your creations out there. You can share your work while still being selective about who gets close to you. Stay focused, trust your intuition, and move with discernment. I’ve spoken before about being cunning—take that in the way it resonates for you.

The numbers I’m getting are 101, 444, 888, and nines. For me, those nines speak to cycles ending. The places that came through are New York, Ohio, Las Vegas, Virginia, D.C., Philadelphia, Texas, and Michigan. Those may be meaningful to some of you, and they may mean nothing to others.

And let me say this plainly: if this reading doesn’t resonate, keep it moving. Don’t come into the comments acting crazy over a message that wasn’t for you. If it does resonate, take a moment with it, do your shadow work, and make the choices that protect your peace.

Stay Savage, Never Average.

text:
1/ Randy Weaver. Ruby Ridge. August 1992.
Iowa farm kid. Army, Fort Bragg. Honorably discharged as a sergeant. Married Vicki. They got deep into end-times Christianity, left Iowa, and built a cabin with no power and no running water on a ridge in northern Idaho. They wanted to be left alone.
He called himself a white separatist. Attended Aryan Nations gatherings nearby. Was not a member. That association is how the government got its hooks in.
2/ 1989: ATF informant (posing as a friend at those gatherings) buys two sawed-off shotguns from Weaver. ATF then offers him a deal: become an informant on Aryan Nations or get charged.
Weaver refuses.
He’s indicted. Arrested January 1991 by a ruse (agents posing as stranded motorists). Released on bond.
Then the clerk error that started the whole thing.
3/ Trial date set for February 1991. A probation officer sends a letter that lists the wrong date: March 20.
Weaver doesn’t show in February. Bench warrant. He stays on the mountain.
For 16 months the Marshals watch the place. They plan how to grab him without a fight.
4/ August 21, 1992.
Six camouflaged U.S. Marshals are on the property doing surveillance. The family dog, Striker, finds them and barks.
Marshals shoot the dog.
What happens next is still disputed. Firefight at a spot they called “the Y.”
Dead:
•  Deputy Marshal William Degan
•  Sammy Weaver, 14 years old, shot in the back while running
•  the dog
DOJ later said they could not determine who fired first.
5/ Sammy’s body is brought back to a shed.
August 22. FBI Hostage Rescue Team is on scene.
They operate under special Rules of Engagement that were later called unconstitutional:
If any adult male is seen with a weapon before a surrender announcement, “deadly force can and should be employed” if the shot won’t hit children.
That’s not the normal FBI deadly-force policy.
6/ FBI sniper Lon Horiuchi.
First shot: hits Randy Weaver in the arm as he, his daughter Sara, and family friend Kevin Harris walk toward the shed where Sammy’s body is.
They run back to the cabin.
Second shot: aimed at Harris as he reaches the door. The bullet goes through the cabin door.
Vicki Weaver is standing behind that door holding their 10-month-old daughter, Elisheba.
The round hits Vicki in the head and kills her. It then wounds Harris.
She is 43.
7/ 11-day siege. Vicki’s body stays in the cabin the whole time.
Hundreds of agents. Armored vehicles. Helicopters.
Bo Gritz (fellow Army SF) is brought in to talk Weaver down.
August 31: Weaver surrenders. Harris is in bad shape. The three surviving daughters walk out.
8/ 1993 trial in Boise.
Government charges murder of the marshal, conspiracy, assault — the works.
Jury acquits Kevin Harris of everything.
Jury acquits Randy Weaver of murder, conspiracy, and the serious counts.
He’s convicted of one thing that stuck: failing to appear on the original gun charge, plus a related bail violation.
18 months (mostly time served). $10,000 fine.
Judge rips the FBI for hiding documents.
9/ 1995: United States government pays the family $3.1 million rather than go to trial on the wrongful-death suit.
$100,000 to Randy. $1 million each to the three daughters.
Harris later settles for $380,000.
Senate hearings. Internal DOJ reports. The special Rules of Engagement get shredded. Several FBI officials get letters of censure. Horiuchi is never convicted.
10/ Randy Weaver later told Congress: if he had it to do over, he would have come down for that court date.
He died May 11, 2022, at 74.
Ruby Ridge is not a cartoon. A man who wouldn’t come to court. A government that sent snipers with shoot-on-sight rules. A 14-year-old boy and a mother holding a baby ended up dead. A jury looked at the murder charges and said no.

The document is offered for sale in one of the Gulf countries.

The appeal was sent a few months before the departure of the French campaign and reveals to history why Mu'allim Yaqub formed a Coptic Legion to protect the Copts.

The historian Muhammad Shafik Ghorbal says that all the indicators and evidence indicated that the French occupation would not last, so Mu'allim Mr.Yaqub knew that the persecution of the Copts was coming.
