text:
A Constitutional and Factual Concern Regarding the Dissolution of the Family Federation

The dissolution of the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification raises important questions concerning both religious freedom and whether all materially relevant facts were sufficiently examined.

On March 4, 2026, the Tokyo High Court upheld the dissolution order, and on June 22, 2026, the Supreme Court dismissed the Federation’s special appeal, allowing the order to become final. The judicial decisions addressed alleged unlawful conduct, including the solicitation of donations under circumstances said to have impaired individuals’ freedom of decision-making.

At the same time, other allegations deserve careful examination. In May 2024, Satoshi Hamada, then a member of the House of Councillors, submitted a formal inquiry concerning allegations of abduction, confinement, and forced religious deconversion involving Family Federation members. The government responded that criminal conduct would be addressed strictly according to law and evidence, while explaining that its dissolution request was based on seven rounds of reporting requests and interviews with relevant persons.

These records do not establish that every allegation of forced deconversion is true. They do establish, however, that such allegations were formally raised before the Diet and required governmental consideration. In a constitutional democracy, serious allegations should neither be dismissed without examination nor treated as established facts without sufficient evidence.

There is also significant disagreement within the Christian community. The United Church of Christ in Japan supported the government’s dissolution request and subsequently supported the Tokyo High Court decision, while expressly acknowledging that Article 20 continues to protect the religious activities of individual members. In 2023, several major Christian organizations likewise issued a joint statement supporting dissolution.

This demonstrates that substantial Christian support for dissolution existed, but it also shows why the constitutional issue should not be reduced to whether the Family Federation’s beliefs are acceptable to other Christians.

Articles 19 and 20 of the Constitution protect freedom of thought, conscience, and religion, while Article 31 protects personal liberty through legally established procedures. Where confinement, coercion, or interference with religious decision-making is alleged, these constitutional protections provide an important framework for examining the facts.

Pastor Haruhisa Nakagawa has offered a different perspective based on his reported experience of entering the organization and examining its activities. He argues that the central ethical emphasis of the Unification Principle includes living for the sake of others and loving one’s enemies. His testimony should not be treated as conclusive, but it represents a perspective that can be considered alongside testimony from critics and former members.

The essential point is the need to distinguish between religious doctrine, organizational conduct, and individual misconduct. A religious teaching cannot automatically be equated with every action of an individual member, just as allegations of unlawful conduct should not be accepted without evidence.

The constitutional concern, therefore, is not whether the Family Federation should be regarded favorably or unfavorably. It is whether all materially relevant evidence—including evidence that challenges the prevailing narrative—has been examined with equal seriousness.

The courts should determine the legality of specific conduct on the basis of evidence and law, rather than determine the legitimacy of a religious worldview according to social or theological preference.

That distinction is essential to preserving both the rule of law and freedom of religion in Japan.

text:
A vital principle for Baptists is that freedom of conscience is a meaningless concession if it does not extend to "freedom of act." Many before had offered religious toleration or liberty of conscience, but still coerced religious acts. Baptists militated against this.

More from the Coldwater Association's Centennial Report in 1874:

"[Our fathers] contested every inch of ground in the hard, unequal struggle with Priest, Magistrate and Statesman, for the inalienable, God-conferred rights of man—freedom of act, of conscience, in choosing a form of worship and the pursuits of happiness. To express these inalienable rights, they used the very significant phrase, "Soul Liberty"—denied the right of the Magistrate to coerce in matters of religion.

God gave them the victory after a long and painful conflict, in which they endured every species of indignity and suffering that ingenuity could invent and power inflict; as whipping, inciting of mobs, imprisonment in county jails, fines, amounting sometimes to more property than they possessed, and banishment under penalty of death.

The victories which they won, were victories for the world. The principles contended for were not stumbled upon, but plainly taught in God's inspired Word and form an article of faith in the creed of Baptists of all ages. . . the name of Baptist should be the synonym of the broadest civil and religious liberty.

But while they left us in possession of this rich heritage, it is not a peaceful possession. We have battles to fight."

Speaking of the period between 1776 and 1876 they wrote, "It is the great emancipation century of the world. Among these great events in our own land, are the separation of Church and State, the right to worship God according to the dictates of conscience and freedom of speech. Without these, what would our throwing off the yoke of a foreign tyrant have been but a change of masters?"

text:
Many years ago, I exchanged letters with an atheist. In the course of our discussion, he made two statements about how the God of Christians was “unfair.”

It isn’t fair, he insisted, that God limits human freedom by imposing rules against various actions and desires.

And it also isn’t fair, he wrote, that God has allowed pain, suffering, and evil in this world. A good God, he argued, wouldn’t allow such things.

It was an example of having one’s cake and eating it, too. Or of having one’s sin and also ignoring the consequences.

Yes, the existence of evil is indeed perplexing, “as painful as it is mysterious,” says the Catechism. But the Christian faith, understood correctly, “constitutes the answer to this question” (CCC, par 309). It is part of the “drama of sin” in which free creatures can either accept or reject the Creator’s gift of love and life.

Of course, skeptics aren’t alone in complaints about divine fairness. I have sometimes thought, with sincere frustration, “This isn’t fair! Why did that happen to me? What is God doing?” On such occasions, the words of God to the prophet Ezekiel are worth contemplating: “Is it my way that is unfair, or rather, are not your ways unfair?”

That question was put forth in the context of a virtuous man who “turns away from virtue to commit iniquity, and dies…” If that man, God told the people, had turned away from wickedness and done what was “right and just,” he would have lived.

We know this is true and right, but we sometimes convince ourselves that we are the exception to the rule. Doesn’t God realize how fortunate he is to have us on his side? Sure, we don’t put it that way—but that’s basically what happens when we question, in one way or another, the very nature of what is good and evil.

It can be tempting to think we have complete autonomy, somehow separate and distinct from God himself.

That temptation was embraced by Adam and Eve when they committed the first sin: “In that sin man preferred himself to God and by that very act scorned him. He chose himself over and against God, against the requirements of his creaturely status and therefore against his own good” (CCC, par 398).

Thus, conversion is necessary; repentance is required.

And that is the heart of the parable of the two sons, uttered by Jesus to the chief priests and elders. Working in the vineyard—that is, the Kingdom—is to pursue the will of God, to seek holiness, and to strive after justice. The parable is simple enough: one son says he will not work, but then changes his mind; the other son gives lip service—“Yes, sir”—but fails to enter the vineyard. The first son, said Jesus, said, “I will not,” but “afterwards changed his mind and went.”

The Greek term used is closely related to the well-known word metanoia, which Saint John Paul II explained is a reference to “a radical change of mind and heart. It is necessary to turn away from evil and to enter the kingdom of justice, love and truth which is being established.”

The first son, in other words, listened to his conscience and then chose to enter the vineyard and to work with his father. This indicates his desire to accept the Father’s gift of divine sonship, to “obtain the glorious liberty of the children of God” (Rom 8:21).

The second son, in the immediate context, represents the Pharisees, who said the right things but failed to do them. Words alone are not enough: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt 7:21).

God created man with free will, and man freely rejected God’s fellowship. But God, through the humility of the Son, offers fellowship again.

Will we gladly enter the vineyard today?

text:
Last night, Cabot’s Homecoming game against Little Rock Christian was interrupted by three separate medical emergencies, beginning when one of the coaches went into cardiac arrest.

My baby girl did what she does as a first responder, and today we know that coach is stable. For that, we are eternally grateful.

But what happened throughout that stadium afterward deserves to be remembered too.

Cabot and Little Rock Christian came together in the end zone. Players and coaches who had spent the evening on opposite sidelines stood together, arms around one another, heads bowed in prayer. In the stands, students did the same.

There is something profoundly grounding about a moment like this. Rivalry has its place. Competition has its place. But when confronted with the fragility of a human life, all of those distinctions become remarkably insignificant.

We spend an extraordinary amount of time talking about everything that divides us. Last night, students in Cabot, Arkansas, offered a quiet reminder that beneath all of it, we are still capable of recognizing our shared humanity, setting aside our differences and turning together toward God.

An entire stadium seemed to understand, without needing to be told, that this was no longer about football.

They came together in prayer.

Some things will always be bigger than football. 🙏

text:
A bank told George E. Johnson no when he asked for two hundred and fifty dollars to start a business, so he went to another branch and said he needed the money for a vacation instead. The banker approved it in thirty minutes.

That vacation loan built the first Black-owned company on the American Stock Exchange and put Afro Sheen in every bathroom cabinet in Black America. He played the system with its own cards and won.

In February of 1954, George E. Johnson walked through the snow on Chicago's South Side to borrow two hundred and fifty dollars.

He had worked ten years in a cosmetics lab. He had developed a formula that could straighten Black men's hair without burning their scalps.

He sat down across from the white loan officer and said he was going to build a great big business.

The officer shuffled his papers, chuckled, and leaned forward. He told Johnson he was doing him a favor by turning him down.

Johnson was twenty-six years old. He had been shining shoes since he was eight.

He had dropped out of Wendell Phillips High School to bus tables during the day and set pins at a bowling alley at night. He had never in his life had anyone do him that kind of favor.

He walked half a block in the cold before the idea hit him.

He turned around, walked past the office that had just rejected him, and went to a different branch of the same bank. This time he did not mention a business.

He told the white loan officer he needed two hundred and fifty dollars to take his wife Joan on a vacation to California.

"I knew this request wouldn't rattle his belief that he was superior to me," Johnson wrote in his memoir decades later. "Nor would it challenge his stereotypes of Black men as subservient or unintelligent."

A Black man wanting to start a company did not fit what the banker believed about the world. A Black man wanting to take his wife on a trip did.

Thirty minutes later, Johnson walked out with a check in his hand.

He never went to California. He took the money, added another two hundred and fifty dollars borrowed from a Chicago barber named Orville Nelson, and started mixing hair relaxer in a South Side storefront.

He called the product Ultra Wave.

He and Joan sold it from the back of their station wagon.

Johnson had been born in 1927 in Richton, Mississippi, in a three-room sharecropper's shack. His parents separated when he was two.

His mother, Priscilla, was eighteen years old when she brought three young sons to Chicago on her own. She earned sixteen dollars a week in a cafeteria.

George started working as soon as he was old enough to carry a shoeshine box. Collecting milk bottles, bussing tables, setting bowling pins.

He was seventeen when he walked into Fuller Products, a Black-owned cosmetics firm run by S. B. Fuller, and found the only mentor he would ever claim.

"I don't know where I would be had it not been for his mentorship," Johnson said. "I left school while in the middle of the 11th grade so I could work. And Fuller inspired me like no one else ever has."

Fuller put him in sales, then the laboratory. A German-born chemist named Herbert Martini worked alongside him.

Together, during off hours, they tried to emulsify a lye-based hair relaxer that would not separate on the shelf. Every emulsifying agent they found in the United States failed.

Martini contacted colleagues in Germany. They shipped compounds that finally held.

That formula, born from a high school dropout and a German immigrant working after hours in a Black-owned lab on the South Side, became Ultra Wave. When Fuller Products turned down the barber Nelson's pitch to produce it, Johnson stepped in.

The vacation loan was next.

Ultra Wave sold to barbershops in Chicago, then Harlem, then across Black neighborhoods in New York. In 1957, Joan repositioned the formula for women and called it Ultra Sheen, a home relaxer that eliminated the need for a hot comb and frequent trips to the beauty shop.

By 1960, Johnson Products held an estimated eighty percent of the Black hair care market.

Then the culture shifted, and Johnson shifted with it. By the late 1960s, the Black Power movement had young people wearing their hair natural.

Johnson did not fight the change.

He made a product for it. Afro Sheen, a spray that left naturals voluminous and glossy, hit the market and became one of the most recognized Black-owned brands in the country.

He hired Black advertising agencies to sell it. Vincent Cullers and Tom Burrell created campaigns that showed Black people in professional careers, in love, in dignity.

Nothing like those images had ever been on American television before.

In 1970, a young Chicago broadcaster named Don Cornelius was trying to take a dance show called Soul Train national.

Nobody would sponsor it. Johnson saw the show, saw the audience, and offered six hundred thousand dollars to put it on the air coast to coast, on one condition: the show had to go national.

Soul Train debuted in syndication on October 2, 1971, with Johnson Products as its first and exclusive national sponsor. The Afro Sheen commercials became almost as famous as the Soul Train Line.

That same year, Johnson Products became the first Black-owned company listed on the American Stock Exchange.

Sales climbed from ten million to thirty-seven million dollars in four years. Johnson built his headquarters at 8522 South Lafayette Avenue, right alongside the Dan Ryan Expressway, deliberately.

He wanted every Black person driving past to see it.

The front plaza had an eleven-foot sculpture by the Black artist Richard Hunt and miniature red brick pyramids that evoked ancient Egypt. Inside, the offices held African sculptures and Herman Miller furniture.

More than five hundred employees worked those halls.

Johnson offered them profit sharing, college tuition reimbursement, paid sick days, maternity leave, and four-day holiday weekends before most companies in America offered any of it.

"I wanted people to know that it was Black-owned," Johnson said. "It was sitting right there in plain sight. You couldn't miss it, and you couldn't deny it."

In November of 1966, Martin Luther King Jr. walked through the front door. King had spent that year living in a Chicago slum to expose the city's housing segregation.

Now he stood in the lobby of a company that employed hundreds and generated millions, anchored to the South Side like a dare. One of his ministers, James Bevel, was with him.

King looked up. He looked down.

He looked at Bevel and said, "Now this is Black Power."

Johnson was standing on the landing above him when he heard it.

"Dr. King used the phrase as a real compliment as he assessed our several floors that were jumping with activity," Johnson recalled in 2025. "Salesmen, chemists, secretaries, a mostly-Black group of employees who were finding their way into America's middle class."

On any given day, Johnson wrote in his memoir, you could walk those halls and come across a Black woman in a white chemist's smock, a Southeast Asian manager, or a young salesman in a suit and an afro.

Then, in 1975, the Federal Trade Commission ordered Johnson Products to place warning labels on Ultra Sheen, because it contained sodium hydroxide. FTC officials assured him that every competitor selling the same chemical would be required to do the same thing.

They were not.

For nearly two years, Ultra Sheen sat on shelves with a government warning while Revlon and every other white-owned competitor sold the same product with no label at all. Revlon's sales representatives told stores that Ultra Sheen was dangerous.

Johnson said it plainly: "It was the same product."

Sales fell. Earnings collapsed from a dollar forty a share to two cents.

The company that a vacation loan had built began to buckle under the weight of a government that had applied the rules unevenly and a market that punished the Black-owned brand first.

The rest came in stages. Johnson and Joan divorced in 1989, and as part of the settlement, she gained controlling interest in the company.

Their son Eric was named president and later resigned. In 1993, Joan sold Johnson Products to IVAX Corporation, a white-owned pharmaceutical company, for sixty-seven million dollars.

Johnson opposed the sale publicly.

Operation PUSH called for a boycott. Community leaders said they felt betrayed.

The company George Johnson had started with a fake vacation loan was no longer Black-owned.

It changed hands again. Carson bought it, then Procter and Gamble in 2004.

In 2009, a group of African American investors bought it back. But, as Johnson put it in his memoir, "like many Black businesses, they eventually ran out of money."

The building at 8522 South Lafayette Avenue is now a charter school called Perspectives Leadership Academy. The eleven-foot sculpture is gone.

The lobby where King looked up and called it Black Power serves a different kind of promise now.

George and Joan remarried in 1995. She died in 2019 at eighty-nine.

He married Madeline Murphy Rabb in 2022. In 2025, at ninety-seven, he published his memoir and called it Afro Sheen.

George E. Johnson died on July 6, 2026, in his downtown Chicago condominium. He was ninety-nine years old.
